analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil and gas drilling leases in the Arctic Ocean.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Natural Resources Committee without a single hearing, markup, or floor vote, despite 49 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare it national policy to keep Arctic Ocean fossil fuels in the ground, and would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Interior Department could not issue or renew any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Sea planning areas [S2][S3]. The stated reasoning is that Arctic drilling is incompatible with avoiding the worst effects of climate change and would threaten fragile Arctic ecosystems that support fisheries, migratory birds, and subsistence hunting [S3]. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be people exposed to climate change risks, coastal communities whose shorelines and fisheries depend on a healthy Arctic marine environment, and Alaska Native and subsistence communities that rely on Arctic ecosystems; the bill's findings cite fisheries, migratory birds, indigenous populations, and subsistence hunters as dependent on those ecosystems [S3]. Future generations would also benefit from fossil fuel reserves never being burned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fisheries, and everyone exposed to climate risk

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea planning areas, permanently removing those waters from drilling [S2][S3].
Makes it national policy to manage the Arctic Ocean in the public interest by keeping fossil fuels in the ground to avoid dangerous climate change impacts [S2][S3].

Protects Arctic ecosystems the bill describes as critical to fisheries, migratory birds, indigenous populations, and subsistence hunters, with no exception for existing or future drilling interests [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to Arctic Ocean leases and any reserves there. The federal government would forgo potential leasing revenue from those waters. Energy consumers could face marginally tighter supply over the long run, though the bill's findings argue that delaying climate action costs far more economically than acting now [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and federal leasing revenue

drawbacks.text: The ban would permanently close a domestic energy resource and forgo federal revenue from Arctic leases, which supporters of drilling argue helps neither consumers nor taxpayers [S3].

A United States-only leasing ban does not stop other Arctic nations, such as Russia, from developing their own Arctic reserves; fuel demand could simply be met from elsewhere, limiting the climate benefit and shifting production to less-regulated waters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is permanent protection of a fragile, hard-to-clean-up marine environment and a large pool of unburned carbon, against forgone domestic oil and gas production and federal leasing revenue. The strongest good-faith objection is that a unilateral ban may not reduce global emissions much if other nations drill their Arctic waters instead. How much it would have mattered depends on how much Arctic oil would otherwise have been economically recoverable, which fell into doubt after oil prices collapsed in 2014-2015 and major companies scaled back Arctic plans.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and sent it to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, but never held a hearing or markup, and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Jared Huffman introduced the bill on September 28, 2015, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S1][S5].
On October 16, 2015, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources; that was the last action of any kind in the bill's history [S5].
The bill accumulated 49 cosponsors, all Democrats, and received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action in the Senate during the remainder of the 114th Congress [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies retained the possibility of Arctic Ocean leases, and no drilling ban or new restrictions on Arctic development became law during the 114th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arctic drilling proponents and the status quo

for.name: Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Arctic Ocean Drilling Act of 2015 and gathered cosponsors for it

for.name: 49 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-controlled in the 114th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 28, 2015 and routed it to the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, then took no further action; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever held

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 49 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and a Republican-controlled committee never moved the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would bar them from ever obtaining or renewing leases or authorizations to explore, develop, or produce oil and gas in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Sea planning areas [S2][S3]. Their interest in opening those waters to drilling runs against the climate and ecosystem protections the bill offered the public.

industries.industry: Arctic fisheries and Alaska Native subsistence communities
industries.note: The bill's findings identify Arctic ecosystems as critical to fisheries and subsistence hunting; keeping drilling out protects the marine environment these groups depend on for their livelihoods and food [S3].
